title: Microscopic Bipartition and Macroscopic Symmetry in a Rényi Entanglement Ensemble
authors: Zhe Wang, Dongxu Liu, Zheng Yan
abstract: Universal information extracted from entanglement at a critical point is commonly associated with the long-distance properties of the bulk state, while microscopic details of a lattice bipartition are expected to be washed out under coarse graining. Counterintuitively, we show directly that such microscopic information can survive in the statistical ensemble that determines the second Rényi entropy and obviously change the physics there. Using quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the square-lattice $J$-$Q_3$ model at the Néel--valence-bond-solid (VBS) transition, we measure magnetic and dimer order parameters in the Rényi-2 ensemble. For a standard axis-aligned bipartition, the VBS component perpendicular to the entanglement boundary remains finite in the thermodynamic extrapolation and is inequivalent to the parallel component, while the Néel order vanishes. For a $45^\circ$ tilted bipartition, in contrast, the two VBS components remain equivalent within numerical accuracy. We interpret this contrast in terms of the Rényi twist defect: the two bipartitions have the same bulk theory but realize different microscopic defect symmetries. Our results demonstrate that lattice information invisible to the bulk continuum theory alone can remain active in the long-distance Rényi ensemble, providing a microscopic explanation for the strong bipartition dependence previously observed in entanglement studies of deconfined criticality.
summary: The authors investigate whether the symmetry of entanglement measured via the Rényi-2 entropy retains microscopic details from the lattice bipartition. Using quantum Monte Carlo simulations on the J-Q3 model, they show that the bipartition geometry dictates the symmetry response of the entanglement ensemble. This proves that the long-distance physics requires both the bulk theory and the specific symmetry constraints imposed by the entanglement defect.
main_problem: To determine if microscopic lattice information, specifically related to the bipartition geometry, can survive and influence the macroscopic symmetry structure of the Rényi entanglement ensemble after coarse-graining, contrasting this with predictions based solely on the bulk continuum theory.
main_result: Microscopic symmetry information encoded in the bipartition is not washed out by coarse-graining; it survives as a macroscopic symmetry response of the Rényi-2 ensemble, demonstrating that the defect structure is crucial.
method: Quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the stochastic-series-expansion method to measure order parameters in the Rényi-2 entanglement ensemble.
model_or_system: The study uses the spin-1/2 square-lattice J-Q3 model, analyzing its behavior near the Néel–valence-bond-solid (VBS) transition.
key_observables: Magnetic order parameter ($|m_z|$), and two components of the columnar VBS order parameter ($|D_x|$ and $|D_y|$).
important_parameters: The entanglement ensemble is studied at a fixed inverse temperature $ eta_E = 2$. The comparison is between standard axis-aligned and $45^\circ$-tilted bipartitions.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the replica representation and the concept of a Rényi twist defect to capture boundary effects.
figures_summary: Figure 2 shows the finite-size dependence of the order parameters for both standard and $45^\circ$-tilted cuts, confirming distinct behaviors. Table I compares thermodynamic-limit constants for different cuts.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the conflict between bulk continuum theory and microscopic lattice details, then uses QMC simulations on the J-Q3 model to measure order parameters for two different bipartitions, concluding that the defect structure dictates the symmetry.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete example of how boundary conditions or local structure (the defect) can impose constraints on emergent long-distance physics (the Rényi ensemble) that are invisible to the continuum theory alone.
